A timed-out request tells you the response never came back, not whether the work got done.

A request that returns a clear error is easy. You know it failed, so you retry it. The hard case is the request that times out with no error. The connection drops, the server dies partway through, or the response is lost on its way back. All three leave the caller holding the same timeout. The only option left is to retry, and a retry is exactly what can run an operation a second time when it already worked the first. When the operation moves money, guessing wrong either way costs: retry something that already succeeded and you charge the customer twice, give up on something that actually worked and the customer has paid for nothing.

This page follows five companies into the same problem. Stripe and AWS are called by outside developers, so their fix is a rule in the API contract itself: send a key. Airbnb and Shopify sit on both sides (their own services call their own payment code), so they build the machinery inside those services. Segment can't ask its callers, phones and third-party devices that won't follow rules, to do anything, so it catches the duplicates downstream instead. Their answers, with the trade-offs each one makes, are compared below.

Every version of this problem reduces to one picture: a call that changes something crosses a network, and there are three places it can die. Only the first is safe to retry, and the caller can't tell the three apart, because all three look identical from the outside: a timeout.

Cause it yourself before reading anyone's answer: cut a $100 charge at each of the three points and decide what the client should do. The rescue tool is an idempotency key, a name the caller picks for the operation and sends unchanged on every retry. Reach for it and a second decision appears: where the server stores that name so it can recognize the retry later. Every failure you can cause here is one the five posts describe.

The row interviewers spend the most time on. Each system's own post names the failure its guarantee doesn't cover - knowing these is what separates using the pattern from understanding it. The red marks in the diagrams above show where each one lives.

Client key hygiene. Reuse an old key for a new charge and the server silently replays the old charge's outcome. The server cannot detect this; correctness depends on key discipline in every integrating codebase.

A reused token with changed parameters. The safest reading is that the customer meant something different, so the service refuses with a validation error naming the mismatch - the guarantee protects intent, and changed parameters are a new intent.

The key’s memory under the guarantee. Key state on a lagging copy brings back the very failure the key was meant to cure - so reads go to the master only. And a mislabeled error: mark a non-retryable failure retryable and the door to double payments reopens, with manual cleanup behind it.
Time. A retry arriving after the ~24-hour window is simply no longer covered. Aggressive timeouts make retries more frequent on purpose, which is only safe while the key machinery is watching.
Pressure on the window. "Almost" exactly once is the honest name: under load the dedupe window shrinks by design, and the 24-hour floor is monitored, not guaranteed.

Anywhere a call that changes something can time out: reserving inventory (over-sell), sending an email (the double send), delivering a webhook (now the receiver's problem), provisioning a machine (AWS's own case), posting a ledger entry. Ask the six questions. The answers move; the wall doesn't.
Five rules that transfer out of these posts into any system you build. Each one is a row of the table, compressed.

Identity is granted, not computed. A fingerprint of the parameters can't tell an accidental repeat from a caller who wants two identical operations. Only the caller knows intent, so the caller (or its SDK) names the operation. Q1

Commit the memory with the work - or design for the moment they part. AWS makes them one all-or-nothing unit; Airbnb slices the request into three all-or-nothing phases; Segment repairs its ledger from the output log after a crash. Nobody leaves the gap unhandled. Q3

The guarantee is only as strong as the key’s memory it sits on. Key state on a lagging copy brings back the exact failure it was built to cure - a few seconds of lag is a double charge. Name where the state lives. Q2

Decide what a duplicate hears. A saved result, a refusal, or silence are all defensible - but the reply's shape decides whether retry-by-default is safe for every caller. It's an API decision, not an accident. Q4
Every key store is a clock. Protection ends - by policy, lease, size, or ~24 hours. Pick the window on purpose, write it down, and page when it thins. Q5
If this comes up in an interview
"The client's request timed out. Did the charge happen?"
"Design an idempotent API for creating orders."

The caller names the operation and sends the same name on every retry. The server remembers the name - and I'd say where: with the work in one commit, or in a separate store with recovery steps, read from the master only. A retry gets the saved result. The memory has a window, so I'd say how long, and what happens after it ends. Then I'd say what still gets through: a reused key, a replica read, a changed parameter, a retry after the window.
